title: Eilik AI robot exposes 8.3M chats and hijack flaws
source_used: The Verge (Cybernews, the pool link, was blocked)
key_facts: The Verge says the servers behind Energize Lab's Eilik AI robot toy (it spells it Eiliko) were left unprotected and store users' conversations on Chinese servers.

Security researcher Sammy Azdoufal could read about 13 million conversations from tens of thousands of people and reach seemingly the whole active fleet of 68,000 toys; over 31,000 profiles in the US belong to children, per the data.
The service reads conversations and builds a profile of each user, including name, age, birthday, profession, family and what kind of person they seem to be, stored with email and IP address.
Energize Lab also stores photos of children and short audio recordings at public web addresses, although its privacy policy says recordings are deleted after processing.
Many admin passwords were on common-password lists.
Azdoufal remotely rewrote the toy's memory and took over its language model from the other side of the world, changing what it said.
Azdoufal plans to publish nine official CVE vulnerability reports for Energize Lab.
The Verge tried for over a month to reach the company through ten addresses; no one answered its questions.
quote_evidence: He could read 13 million conversations from tens of thousands of people.

Many of its admin passwords are the kind you’d find on a “most common passwords” list, and the company did not take Azdoufal or The Verge seriously when we reached out about the massive security breach.
In the end, not a single person stepped forward to answer our questions.
why_it_matters_hint: A toy marketed to families kept children's private chats on servers that anyone who found the flaw could read or take over.
event_date: The Verge investigation published 15 Oct 2026; Cybernews report 16 Oct 2026
notes: Cybernews (pool link, 'Eilik AI robot exposes 8.3M chats') was blocked (403); The Verge's own investigation of the same toy was read instead. Counts differ: Verge says about 13 million conversations; Cybernews' headline says 8.3 million chats. The 8.3 million figure is unconfirmed and not used. The Verge spells the product Eiliko in places.
